rationale: B wins because it keeps one hand on the evidence and the other on the reporter's objections. A's "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" may be true, but it is not in the supplied update; B's "Without the fee schedule this angle cannot be pitched" is the discipline a founder needs before sending anything. B has fewer angles, but fewer loose wires.
gaps_in_A: "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" imports a historical claim the update did not supply; flagging proof later does not launder it into a grounded angle.
"FedNow policy/infrastructure-adoption angle ... duplicate" throws away a genuinely distinct rail-adoption story; FedNow as protagonist is not the same as Plaid versus card networks.

"every angle here is currently unprovable without one" overcorrects on the missing merchant problem; the counterposition and FedNow angles need proof, but not necessarily a named launch customer to exist.
"routing merchant payments through instant, FedNow-based settlement" risks conflating Plaid's 12,000 institution connections with actual FedNow reach before the set proves that subset.
gaps_in_B: "A flat fee is worse than a percentage on small tickets and better on large ones" states the math too confidently without Plaid's flat fee or the real card-fee schedule.

"puts bank-to-bank payments in front of shoppers" reaches slightly beyond the facts; the update says merchants can accept account-to-account payments, not what the shopper checkout experience looks like.
"Plaid turns 12,000 bank connections into a payments network" as a duplicate is too quick; network reach could be a separate infrastructure angle if FedNow-enabled coverage is proven.
